content: 1. A randomized controlled clinical trial conducted in Senegal evaluated the effects of vitamin A supplementation on malnourished children. The study compared the outcomes of a single high dose versus daily low doses of vitamin A on morbidity in hospitalized children. (Eur J Clin Nutr, 2007; 61:1393–9) 2. Donnen et al. performed a placebo-controlled trial to assess the impact of high-dose versus low-dose vitamin A on the morbidity of malnourished children in hospitals. (Am J Clin Nutr, 1998; 68:1254–60) 3. Sattar et al. investigated the efficacy of combining high-dose vitamin A with daily low-dose supplementation in children suffering from severe acute malnutrition and other illnesses. (PLoS One, 2012; 7:e33112) 4. Julien et al. conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Mozambican children hospitalized with non-measles acute lower respiratory tract infections to evaluate the role of vitamin A. (Trop Med Int Health, 1999; 4:794–800) 5. Nacul et al. studied the efficacy of vitamin A treatment in non-measles childhood pneumonia through a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. (BMJ, 1997; 315:505–10) 6. Kjolhede et al. explored the use of vitamin A as an adjuvant treatment for lower respiratory tract infections in a clinical trial. (J Pediatr, 1995; 126:807–12) 7. Dibley et al. found that vitamin A supplementation did not reduce the incidence of acute respiratory illness and diarrhea in preschool-aged Indonesian children. (J Nutr, 1996; 126:434–42) 8. D’Souza et al. demonstrated that a high dose of vitamin A reduced childhood mortality in high-risk populations. (BMJ, 1992; 304:207–10) 9. Fawzi et al. examined the effects of vitamin A supplementation on diarrheal and respiratory tract infections among children in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. (J Pediatr, 2000; 137:660–7) 10. The World Health Organization published a manual for physicians and senior health workers on the treatment of diarrhea, emphasizing evidence-based management strategies. (Geneva: WHO, 2005) 11. Lima et al. investigated the etiologies and interactions of persistent diarrhea with malnutrition in children in Northeast Brazil. (Acta Paediatr, 1992; 81:39–44) 12. Patwari reviewed the interaction between diarrhea and malnutrition, highlighting the bidirectional relationship. (Indian J Pediatr, 1999; 66 Suppl) 13. Suh et al. discussed recent advances in oral rehydration therapy (ORT), focusing on its role in managing dehydration. (Electrolyte Blood Press, 2010; 8:82–6) 14. Moore et al. demonstrated that prolonged episodes of acute diarrhea negatively impact growth and increase the risk of persistent diarrhea in children. (Gastroenterology, 2010; 139:1156–64) 15. UNICEF and WHO published a report on why children continue to die from diarrhea and outlined actionable solutions. (Geneva: UNICEF/WHO, 2009) 16. Manary et al. systematically reviewed the care of children with diarrhea in community-based management of severe acute malnutrition. (PDF) 17. Cilberto et al. compared home-based therapy using ready-to-use therapeutic food with standard therapy for treating malnourished Malawian children. (Am J Clin Nutr, 2005; 81:864–70) 18. Heikens et al. evaluated the effects of high-energy supplements and metronidazole on morbidity and growth in malnourished children rehabilitated in the community. (Eur J Clin Nutr, 1993; 47:174–91) 19. Ribeiro et al. studied the treatment of acute diarrhea with oral rehydration solutions containing glutamine. (J Am Coll Nutr, 1994; 13:251–5) 20. Lima and Guerrant questioned the necessity of glutamine supplementation for childhood malnutrition. (J Pediatr Gastroenterol Nutr, 2005; 40:526–7) 21. Sondheimer argued that glutamine supplementation is likely unnecessary for childhood malnutrition. (J Pediatr Gastroenterol Nutr, 2005; 40:24–5) 22. Kerac et al. conducted the PRONUT study, a double-blind efficacy trial of probiotics and prebiotics for severe acute malnutrition in Malawi. (Lancet, 2009; 374:136–44) 23. Basu et al. demonstrated the efficacy of high-dose Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG in controlling acute watery diarrhea in Indian children. (J Clin Gastroenterol, 2009; 43:208–13) 24. Lazzerini and Ronfani reviewed the use of oral zinc supplementation for treating diarrhea in children. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2012; 6:CD005436) 25. Doherty et al. found that higher-dose zinc regimens during rehabilitation from severe protein-energy malnutrition were associated with increased mortality. (Am J Clin Nutr, 1998; 68:742–8) 26. James explored the effects of protein-calorie malnutrition on intestinal absorption and jejunal disaccharidase activities in children. (Ann N Y Acad Sci, 1971; 176:244–61) 27. The Southampton Health Technology Assessment Centre systematically reviewed interventions for treating severe acute malnutrition in young children. (University of Southampton, 2011) 28. Nurko et al. successfully used a chicken-based diet to treat severely malnourished children with persistent diarrhea. (J Pediatr, 1997; 131:405–12) 29. Bhutta et al. compared nutrient absorption and weight gain in children with persistent diarrhea using a rice-lentil/yogurt/milk diet versus soy formula. (J Pediatr Gastroenterol Nutr, 1994; 18:45–52) 30. Amadi et al. demonstrated improved nutritional recovery with an elemental diet in Zambian children with persistent diarrhea and malnutrition. (J Trop Pediatr, 2005; 51:5–10) 31. Bhandari et al. showed that daily zinc supplementation significantly reduced severe diarrheal morbidity in young North Indian children. (Pediatrics, 2002; 109:e86) 32. Sazawal et al. demonstrated the efficacy of zinc supplementation in young children with acute diarrhea in India. (N Engl J Med, 1995; 333:839–44) 33. Roy et al. evaluated the impact of zinc supplementation on persistent diarrhea in malnourished Bangladeshi children. (Acta Paediatr, 1998; 87:1235–9) 34. Maitland et al. investigated mortality after fluid bolus administration in African children with severe infection. (N Engl J Med, 2011; 364:2483–95) 35. Heikens et al. addressed the challenges of managing HIV-infected, severely malnourished children in high-prevalence areas. (Lancet, 2008; 371:1305–7) 36. Kim et al. found that prompt initiation of antiretroviral therapy with therapeutic food improved outcomes in HIV-infected Malawian children with malnutrition. (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr, 2012; 59:173–6)
